claim: Cpt1c knock-out (KO) mice show motor function deficits, such as ataxia, dyscoordination, and muscle weakness.
source: Cpt1c KO mice show motor function deficits, such as ataxia, dyscoordination, and muscle weakness (Carrasco et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Carrasco et al., 2013

claim: Cpt1c KO mice show learning deficits.
source: Cpt1c KO mice show motor function deficits, such as ataxia, dyscoordination, and muscle weakness (Carrasco et al., 2013), in addition to learning deficits (Carrasco et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Carrasco et al., 2012

claim: Cpt1c KO mice show impaired hypothalamic control of body energy homeostasis.
source: Cpt1c KO mice show motor function deficits, such as ataxia, dyscoordination, and muscle weakness (Carrasco et al., 2013), in addition to learning deficits (Carrasco et al., 2012) and impaired hypothalamic control of body energy homeostasis (Casals et al., 2016; Pozo et al., 2017; Rodríguez-Rodríguez et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Casals et al., 2016; Pozo et al., 2017; Rodríguez-Rodríguez et al., 2019

claim: Two CPT1C mutations have been associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) in humans.
source: Interestingly, the unique two CPT1C mutations described in humans to date have been associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) (Hong et al., 2019; Rinaldi et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hong et al., 2019 and Rinaldi et al., 2015

claim: HSPs are a group of inherited neurological disorders characterized by slowly progressive weakness and spasticity of the muscles of the legs, caused by axonopathy of corticospinal motor neurons.
source: HSPs are a group of inherited neurological disorders characterized by slowly progressive weakness and spasticity of the muscles of the legs, caused by axonopathy of corticospinal motor neurons (Blackstone et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Blackstone et al., 2011

claim: Impairment in organelle transport along the axon is a common trait in the development of HSP.
source: Of note, Impairment in organelle transport along the axon is a common trait in the development of the disease (Boutry et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutry et al., 2019

claim: Cpt1c KO neurons have shorter axons (about a 40% length reduction) compared to WT neurons at 4 days in vitro.
source: Cultured cortical neurons derived from wild type (WT) and Cpt1cKO mice were analyzed at 4 days of in vitro division (DIV) and we observed that Cpt1cKO neurons had shorter axons (about a 40% length reduction) compared to WT neurons (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Axon length in Cpt1c KO neurons is rescued by CPT1C re-expression but not by CPT1CR37C or CPT1CM589S.
source: Axon length was rescued by CPT1C re-expression but not by CPT1CR37C or CPT1CM589S (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The binding of malonyl-CoA to CPT1C is required for proper axon growth.
source: Axon length was rescued by CPT1C re-expression but not by CPT1CR37C or CPT1CM589S (Figure 1B). These results suggested that the binding of malonyl-CoA to CPT1C is required for proper axon growth
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1CM589S (which cannot bind malonyl-CoA) does not rescue axon length

claim: CPT1CM589S overexpression in WT cultures reduces axon length.
source: Accordingly, CPT1CM589S overexpression in WT cultures reduced axon length (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: CPT1C is necessary but not sufficient for promoting axon growth.
source: Of note, CPT1C overexpression in WT cultures was not enough to increase axon length, indicating that CPT1C is necessary but not sufficient for promoting axon growth
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1C overexpression does not increase axon length beyond WT levels

claim: Dendritic arborization is diminished in Cpt1c KO neurons compared to WT cells at 4DIV.
source: We also analysed dendritic arborization at 4DIV and found that it was diminished in Cpt1cKO neurons compared to WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: The percentage of polarized cells is reduced in Cpt1c KO cultures.
source: Moreover, the percentage of polarized cells (cells with a defined axon between the neurites) was reduced, and the percentage of cells without any neurite was increased in Cpt1c KO cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: The percentage of cells without any neurite is increased in Cpt1c KO cultures.
source: Moreover, the percentage of polarized cells (cells with a defined axon between the neurites) was reduced, and the percentage of cells without any neurite was increased in Cpt1c KO cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: CPT1C overexpression in WT neurons is not enough to increase dendritic arborization.
source: CPT1C overexpression in WT neurons was not enough to increase dendritic arborization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), as observed with axon growth
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: CPT1C is necessary for proper axon growth, cell polarization and dendritic arborization.
source: In summary, our results indicate that CPT1C is necessary for proper axon growth, cell polarization and dendritic arborization
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing deficits in Cpt1c KO neurons

claim: Glucose depletion increases ACC phosphorylation in WT and Cpt1c KO neurons.
source: We checked that glucose depletion or AICAR treatment increased ACC phosphorylation, as indicative of malonyl-CoA synthesis inhibition (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: AICAR treatment increases ACC phosphorylation in WT and Cpt1c KO neurons.
source: We checked that glucose depletion or AICAR treatment increased ACC phosphorylation, as indicative of malonyl-CoA synthesis inhibition (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Glucose depletion, AICAR treatment, and TOFA treatment reduce axon length in WT cortical neurons.
source: All the treatments reduced axon length in WT cortical neurons suggesting a key role for malonyl-CoA in the regulation of axon growth (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Glucose depletion, AICAR treatment, and TOFA treatment do not further reduce axon length in Cpt1c KO neurons.
source: However, none of the treatments were able to further reduce axon length in Cpt1c KO neurons, pointing to CPT1C as a mediator of the malonyl-CoA effects
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no additional reduction in axon length in KO neurons

claim: CPT1C is a mediator of malonyl-CoA effects on axon growth.
source: However, none of the treatments were able to further reduce axon length in Cpt1c KO neurons, pointing to CPT1C as a mediator of the malonyl-CoA effects
evidence: Inferred from the observation that treatments reducing malonyl-CoA do not affect axon length in CPT1C-deficient neurons

claim: CPT1C interacts with protrudin in HeLa cells.
source: With the GFP-Trap assay, protrudin was able to co-immunoprecipitate CPT1C (Figure 3A), confirming the interaction between these two proteins
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A

claim: CPT1C interacts with protrudin as demonstrated by FRET analysis.
source: Results shown in Figure 3B–C confirm that CPT1C is able to interact with protrudin
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: The interaction between CPT1C and protrudin is not affected by glucose availability.
source: The interaction between CPT1C and protrudin was not affected by glucose availability (Figure 3E) or the inhibition of malonyl-CoA synthesis (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The interaction between CPT1C and protrudin is not affected by the inhibition of malonyl-CoA synthesis.
source: The interaction between CPT1C and protrudin was not affected by glucose availability (Figure 3E) or the inhibition of malonyl-CoA synthesis (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F

claim: CPT1C overexpression favors a more peripheral location of LE/Lys compared to control cells.
source: Figure 4 demonstrates that CPT1C overexpression favoured a more peripheral location of LE/Lys compared to control cells, a phenotype similar to protrudin overexpression
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4

claim: The percentage of cells with Lamp1 in the protrusion tips increases from 28% in control cells to 76% in CPT1C-overexpressing cells.
source: Specifically, the percentage of cells with Lamp1 in the protrusion tips increased from 28% in control cells (mTurquoise-ER-transfected cells) to 76% in CPT1C-overexpressing cells
evidence: Supported by quantification of microscopy data

claim: CPT1CM589S expression does not trigger any change in LE/Lys distribution compared to control cells.
source: In contrast, the expression of CPT1CM589S did not trigger any change in LE/Lys distribution compared to control cells
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing no change in Lamp1 distribution

claim: TOFA treatment reduces intracellular malonyl-CoA levels in HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, the treatment of cells with TOFA for 1 hr, which drastically reduced the level of malonyl-CoA (Figure 4A), was enough to avoid the peripheral distribution of LE/Lys in CPT1C-overexpresssing cells
evidence: Supported by malonyl-CoA measurement data shown in Figure 4A

claim: TOFA treatment prevents the peripheral distribution of LE/Lys in CPT1C-overexpressing cells.
source: Interestingly, the treatment of cells with TOFA for 1 hr, which drastically reduced the level of malonyl-CoA (Figure 4A), was enough to avoid the peripheral distribution of LE/Lys in CPT1C-overexpresssing cells, but not in cells that overexpressed protrudin (Figure 4B–C)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B–C

claim: TOFA treatment does not prevent the peripheral distribution of LE/Lys in protrudin-overexpressing cells.
source: Interestingly, the treatment of cells with TOFA for 1 hr, which drastically reduced the level of malonyl-CoA (Figure 4A), was enough to avoid the peripheral distribution of LE/Lys in CPT1C-overexpresssing cells, but not in cells that overexpressed protrudin (Figure 4B–C)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B–C

claim: Cell circularity is increased by TOFA treatment in CPT1C-overexpressing cells.
source: Moreover, cell circularity was increased by TOFA treatment in CPT1C-overexpressing cells (Figure 4D), which is indicative of decreased protrusion formation
evidence: Supported by circularity analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: CPT1C overexpression favors anterograde transport of LE/Lys.
source: These analyses showed that CPT1C overexpression favored anterograde transport of LE/Lys, but had no effect on retrograde transport
evidence: Supported by live tracking data of mCherry-FYCO1 vesicles

claim: CPT1C overexpression has no effect on retrograde transport of LE/Lys.
source: These analyses showed that CPT1C overexpression favored anterograde transport of LE/Lys, but had no effect on retrograde transport
evidence: Supported by live tracking data showing no change in retrograde parameters

claim: CPT1C overexpression increases the anterograde moving distance of LE/Lys.
source: Specifically, CPT1C overexpression increased the anterograde moving distance (Figure 5A–B), while not modifying the velocity (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by live tracking data shown in Figure 5A–B

claim: CPT1C overexpression does not modify the velocity of anterograde LE/Lys transport.
source: Specifically, CPT1C overexpression increased the anterograde moving distance (Figure 5A–B), while not modifying the velocity (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by live tracking data shown in Figure 5C

claim: TOFA treatment reduces the moving distance, velocity and directionality of LE/Lys in CPT1C-expressing cells.
source: TOFA treatment reduced the moving distance, velocity and the directionality only in CPT1C-expressing cells (Figure 5A–E)
evidence: Supported by live tracking data shown in Figure 5A–E

claim: CPT1CM589S expression reduces the anterograde moving distance and velocity of mCherry-FYCO1 vesicles to the same extent as TOFA treatment.
source: As expected, CPT1CM589S expression reduced the anterograde moving distance and velocity of mCherry-FYCO1 vesicles to the same extent as TOFA treatment
evidence: Supported by live tracking data comparing CPT1CM589S to TOFA treatment

claim: CPT1C senses malonyl-CoA and regulates anterograde transport of LE/Lys.
source: These results indicate that CPT1C senses malonyl-CoA and regulates anterograde transport of LE/Lys
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing CPT1C effects depend on malonyl-CoA

claim: When malonyl-CoA levels are high, the anterograde transport of LE/Lys is promoted.
source: When malonyl-CoA levels are high, the anterograde transport is promoted, but when they decrease, the plus-end motility of FYCO1-positive vesicles is slowed down or inhibited
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing CPT1C promotes transport under normal conditions but not when malonyl-CoA is reduced

claim: When malonyl-CoA levels decrease, the plus-end motility of FYCO1-positive vesicles is slowed down or inhibited.
source: When malonyl-CoA levels are high, the anterograde transport is promoted, but when they decrease, the plus-end motility of FYCO1-positive vesicles is slowed down or inhibited
evidence: Supported by experiments showing TOFA treatment reduces vesicle motility

claim: CPT1C is localized in the ER.
source: Confocal microscopy confirmed the localization of CPT1C in the ER, using VAPA as an ER marker
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization with VAPA

claim: CPT1C is found in ER-lysosome contact sites partly colocalizing with protrudin.
source: Moreover, CPT1C was found in ER-lysosome contact sites partly colocalizing with protrudin
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6

claim: CPT1C is not enriched in ER-lysosome contact sites compared to protrudin.
source: CPT1C was not enriched in contact sites compared to protrudin, which was highly enriched there
evidence: Supported by intensity line plot analysis in Figure 6B

claim: CPT1C does not form ER-lysosome contact sites, but serves as a regulator of their function.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that CPT1C does not form the contact sites, but serves as a regulator of their function
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1C is present but not enriched at contact sites

claim: Protrudin silencing in CPT1C-expressing cells highly reduces the percentage of cells with Lamp1 in the periphery.
source: Protrudin silencing in CPT1C-expressing cells highly reduced the percentage of cells with Lamp1 in the periphery (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A

claim: CPT1C effects on LE/Lys distribution are mediated, at least partially, by protrudin.
source: These results indicate that CPT1C effects are mediated, at least partially, by protrudin
evidence: Inferred from the observation that protrudin silencing reduces CPT1C effects

claim: The reduction in peripheral Lamp1 driven by protrudin silencing is similar to the reduction observed by TOFA treatment.
source: Interestingly, the reduction driven by protrudin silencing was similar to the reduction observed by TOFA treatment (Figure 7B), and TOFA did not show any further effect in protrudin-silenced cells
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B

claim: TOFA does not show any further effect on peripheral Lamp1 in protrudin-silenced cells.
source: Interestingly, the reduction driven by protrudin silencing was similar to the reduction observed by TOFA treatment (Figure 7B), and TOFA did not show any further effect in protrudin-silenced cells
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing no additive effect

claim: Malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis and protrudin share the same signalling pathway.
source: These data suggest that malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis and protrudin share the same signalling pathway
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TOFA and protrudin silencing have similar non-additive effects

claim: The fraction of Lamp1 overlapping with protrudin is not changed by CPT1C-overexpression or TOFA treatment.
source: The results showed that the fraction of Lamp1 or Rab7 overlapping with protrudin was neither changed by CPT1C-overexpression nor by TOFA treatment (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, respectively)
evidence: Supported by Manders overlap coefficient analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: The fraction of Rab7 overlapping with protrudin is not changed by CPT1C-overexpression or TOFA treatment.
source: The results showed that the fraction of Lamp1 or Rab7 overlapping with protrudin was neither changed by CPT1C-overexpression nor by TOFA treatment (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, respectively)
evidence: Supported by Manders overlap coefficient analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: Protrudin-mediated ER-LE/Lys contacts are not regulated by the malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis.
source: The results showed that the fraction of Lamp1 or Rab7 overlapping with protrudin was neither changed by CPT1C-overexpression nor by TOFA treatment (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, respectively), indicating that protrudin-mediated ER-LE/Lys contacts are not regulated by the malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis
evidence: Inferred from the observation that contact site formation is unchanged by CPT1C or malonyl-CoA manipulation

claim: CPT1C overexpression reduces protrudin-association with kinesin-1 (KIF5B).
source: Interestingly, CPT1C overexpression reduced protrudin-association with kinesin-1, but CPT1CM589S did not (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D

claim: CPT1CM589S does not reduce protrudin-association with kinesin-1.
source: Interestingly, CPT1C overexpression reduced protrudin-association with kinesin-1, but CPT1CM589S did not (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D

claim: The malonyl-CoA bound conformation of CPT1C favours kinesin-1 transfer from ER-bound protrudin to LE/Lys.
source: These results suggest that the malonyl-CoA bound conformation of CPT1C favours kinesin-1 transfer from ER-bound protrudin to LE/Lys
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1C reduces kinesin-1 on protrudin while increasing it on vesicles, but CPT1CM589S does not

claim: CPT1C overexpression enhances the intensity of kinesin-1 in Lamp1-positive vesicles.
source: To verify this notion, we analyzed the intensity of kinesin-1 in Lamp1-positive vesicles and found that it was enhanced by CPT1C overexpression, while the concomitant treatment with TOFA blocked that increase (Figure 7E)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7E

claim: TOFA treatment blocks the CPT1C-mediated increase in kinesin-1 intensity at Lamp1-positive vesicles.
source: To verify this notion, we analyzed the intensity of kinesin-1 in Lamp1-positive vesicles and found that it was enhanced by CPT1C overexpression, while the concomitant treatment with TOFA blocked that increase (Figure 7E)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7E

claim: CPT1C increases kinesin-1 recruitment to FYCO1-positive vesicles.
source: Moreover, in cells overexpressing FYCO1, CPT1C increased kinesin-1 recruitment to FYCO1-positive vesicles, but not when the FYCO1 mutant (∆735–773) that lacks the kinesin-1-binding domain was used (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: CPT1C does not increase kinesin-1 recruitment to FYCO1 mutant (∆735–773) that lacks the kinesin-1-binding domain.
source: Moreover, in cells overexpressing FYCO1, CPT1C increased kinesin-1 recruitment to FYCO1-positive vesicles, but not when the FYCO1 mutant (∆735–773) that lacks the kinesin-1-binding domain was used (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: CPT1C enhances protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to FYCO1 at LE/Lys only in the presence of malonyl-CoA.
source: In summary, the overall results indicate that CPT1C enhances protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to FYCO1 at LE/Lys only in the presence of malonyl-CoA
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing CPT1C effects on kinesin-1 transfer depend on malonyl-CoA

claim: The mean intensity of Lamp1 in Cpt1c KO neurons is reduced compared to WT cells at the axon tip.
source: Results showed that the mean intensity of Lamp1 in Cpt1cKO neurons was reduced compared to WT cells (Figure 8B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8B

claim: CPT1C re-expression in KO neurons restores the mean intensity of Lamp1 at the axon tip.
source: Moreover, CPT1C re-expression in KO neurons restored the mean intensity of Lamp1 at the axon tip (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: Glucose deprivation, AICAR or TOFA treatment diminishes Lamp1 mean intensity at growth cones in WT neurons.
source: Glucose deprivation, AICAR or TOFA treatment diminished Lamp1 mean intensity at growth cones in WT neurons, but none of the treatments was able to further decrease it in Cpt1c KO cells, in accordance with the measurements of axon length (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Glucose deprivation, AICAR or TOFA treatment does not further decrease Lamp1 mean intensity at growth cones in Cpt1c KO neurons.
source: Glucose deprivation, AICAR or TOFA treatment diminished Lamp1 mean intensity at growth cones in WT neurons, but none of the treatments was able to further decrease it in Cpt1c KO cells, in accordance with the measurements of axon length (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing no additional reduction in KO neurons

claim: In non-treated WT neurons, Lamp1 intensity at the tip is highly increased compared to the rest of the axon.
source: In non-treated WT neurons, Lamp1 intensity at the tip was highly increased compared to the rest of the axon (Figure 8C)
evidence: Supported by linear fluorescence profile analysis shown in Figure 8C

claim: In treated WT neurons or Cpt1c KO neurons, Lamp1 intensity is very similar throughout the axon.
source: By contrast, in treated WT neurons or Cpt1c KO neurons Lamp1 intensity was very similar throughout the axon
evidence: Supported by linear fluorescence profile analysis shown in Figure 8C

claim: Energy stress that decreases malonyl-CoA levels causes a CPT1C-mediated reduction in the number of LE/Lys that reach the axon tip.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that energy stress that decreases malonyl-CoA levels causes a CPT1C-mediated reduction in the number of LE/Lys that reach the axon tip, resulting in axon growth arrest
evidence: Summarizes findings from experiments showing reduced Lamp1 at axon tips under energy stress

claim: Exogenous malonyl-CoA increases intracellular malonyl-CoA levels in HeLa cells.
source: We first checked that malonyl-CoA was able to penetrate the cells and increase its intracellular levels (Figure 9A), as previously described (Knobloch et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by malonyl-CoA measurement data shown in Figure 9A and citation to Knobloch et al., 2017

claim: Exogenous malonyl-CoA partially reverses Lamp1 intensity decrease at the axon tip caused by glucose depletion or TOFA treatment.
source: Figure 9B shows that exogenous malonyl-CoA was enough to partially reverse Lamp1 intensity decrease at the axon tip, caused by glucose depletion or TOFA treatment (a tendency was observed in AICAR treated cells)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9B

claim: Exogenous malonyl-CoA partially restores axon growth under glucose depletion, AICAR, or TOFA treatment.
source: Moreover, axon growth was partially restored in all conditions (Figure 9C)
evidence: Supported by axon length measurements shown in Figure 9C

claim: Malonyl-CoA does not cause any effect on Lamp1 intensity or axon growth in CPT1C deficient cells.
source: However, malonyl-CoA did not cause any effect in CPT1C deficient cells
evidence: Supported by data showing no rescue in KO neurons

claim: The malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis is an important regulator of LE/Lys anterograde transport and axon growth in response to energy stress.
source: We conclude that the malonyl-CoA/CPT1C axis is an important regulator of LE/Lys anterograde transport and axon growth in response to energy stress
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing malonyl-CoA and CPT1C regulate LE/Lys transport and axon growth

claim: CPT1C is a new regulator of LE/Lys anterograde transport in neurons.
source: Collectively our data demonstrate that CPT1C is a new regulator of LE/Lys anterograde transport in neurons
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments demonstrating CPT1C's role in LE/Lys transport

claim: Under sufficient nutrient supply, CPT1C senses intracellular malonyl-CoA levels and promotes the plus-end transport of LE/Lys through the enhancement of protrudin function.
source: Under sufficient nutrient supply, CPT1C will sense intracellular malonyl-CoA levels and promote the plus-end transport of LE/Lys through the enhancement of protrudin function
evidence: Summarizes findings showing CPT1C promotes transport under normal conditions

claim: Under energy stresses, malonyl-CoA synthesis is inhibited, and the malonyl-CoA-unbound CPT1C prevents the protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to LE/Lys.
source: By contrast, under energy stresses, such as glucose depletion or AMPK activation, malonyl-CoA synthesis will be inhibited, and the malonyl-CoA-unbound CPT1C will prevent the protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to LE/Lys
evidence: Summarizes findings showing CPT1C does not promote transport under energy stress

claim: Under energy stress, axon growth in neurons is temporarily arrested.
source: As a consequence, axon growth in neurons will be temporarily arrested (see Figure 10 for a scheme)
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing reduced axon growth under energy stress

claim: CPT1C is needed for proper dendrite growth.
source: Our results also show that CPT1C is needed for proper dendrite growth, since CPT1C KO neurons showed poor arborisation
evidence: Supported by dendritic arborization analysis showing deficits in KO neurons

claim: CPT1C's role in dendrite arborization is not mediated by protrudin.
source: However, we do not think this effect is mediated by protrudin, since it has been demonstrated that protrudin promotes the growth of axon but not of dendrites (Hashimoto et al., 2014)
evidence: Inferred from citation showing protrudin does not affect dendrites

claim: CPT1C could play a role in dendrite arborization through a mechanism independent of protrudin.
source: Therefore, we believe that CPT1C could play a role in dendrite arborization through a mechanism independent of protrudin
evidence: Speculative statement based on inference from protrudin's known functions

claim: The presence of nutrients in the media increases intracellular malonyl-CoA in addition to amino acids.
source: The presence of nutrients in the media will increase intracellular malonyl-CoA in addition to amino acides, and in consequence favours mobile LE/Lys to move towards the periphery for mTORC activation, local cell growth and membrane expansion, which is of special importance during neuron development
evidence: Based on established knowledge of nutrient metabolism

claim: Upon starvation, the intracellular decrease of malonyl-CoA and amino acids stops the plus-end transport to save energy and facilitate fusion with autophagosomes.
source: By contrast, upon starvation, the intracellular decrease of malonyl-CoA and amino acids will stop the plus-end transport in order to save energy and facilitate their fusion with autophagosomes
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings and established knowledge of starvation responses

claim: CPT1C is unlikely to regulate protrudin-mediated LE/Lys positioning in response to changes in amino acids.
source: Since malonyl-CoA levels depend on the metabolism of fatty acids and glucose, but not on amino acids (Wolfgang and Lane, 2006), CPT1C is unlikely to regulate protrudin-mediated LE/Lys positioning in response to changes in amino acids
evidence: Inferred from citation showing malonyl-CoA does not depend on amino acids

claim: Amino acid mediated activation of PI3P production regulates protrudin-mediated LE/Lys positioning.
source: Instead, amino acid mediated activation of PI3P production has been shown to play such a role (Hong et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2017

claim: Mitochondria are targeted into actively extending axons to supply ATP necessary for axon growth.
source: In growing neurons, mitochondria are also targeted into actively extending axons, in order to supply ATP necessary for this high energy consuming process (Sheng, 2017; Smith and Gallo, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sheng, 2017 and Smith and Gallo, 2018

claim: LE/Lys act as mRNA translation platforms for the synthesis of new proteins necessary to sustain mitochondria function in axons.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that LE/Lys also act as mRNA translation platforms for the synthesis of new proteins necessary to sustain mitochondria function in axons (Cioni et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cioni et al., 2019

claim: LE/Lys anterograde transport is necessary for axon growth, either for rapid membrane expansion, or to provide platforms for local protein synthesis.
source: Collectively, data from the literature indicate that LE/Lys anterograde transport is necessary for axon growth, either for rapid membrane expansion, or to provide platforms for local protein synthesis
evidence: Summarizes findings from cited literature

claim: Malonyl-CoA is a derivative of glucose catabolism used for fatty acid synthesis.
source: Malonyl-CoA is a derivative of glucose catabolism used for fatty acid synthesis
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: Malonyl-CoA levels highly fluctuate depending on the feeding or fasting state of the individual.
source: Its levels highly fluctuate depending on the feeding or fasting state of the individual
evidence: Based on established knowledge of metabolic regulation

claim: In the brain cortex, malonyl-CoA levels are 9 times higher after feeding than under fasting conditions.
source: Specifically in the brain cortex, malonyl-CoA levels are 9 times higher after feeding than under fasting conditions (Tokutake et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tokutake et al., 2010

claim: Malonyl-CoA levels are tightly controlled by AMPK.
source: Malonyl-CoA levels are tightly controlled by AMPK
evidence: Based on established knowledge of AMPK pathway

claim: AICAR treatment of newly plated hippocampal neurons results in KIF5 phosphorylation and the prevention of PI3K enrichment at the neurite tip.
source: AICAR treatment of newly platted hippocampal neurons resulted in KIF5 phosphorylation and the prevention of PI3K enrichment at the neurite tip, which was necessary for proper axon growth (Amato et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Amato et al., 2011

claim: ACC phosphorylation and the consequent depletion of malonyl-CoA levels is a downstream pathway of AMPK activation.
source: Our results identify another downstream pathway of AMPK activation, which is ACC phosphorylation and the consequent depletion of malonyl-CoA levels
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing AMPK activation leads to ACC phosphorylation and reduced malonyl-CoA

claim: AMPK is activated by metabolic stresses (fasting, exercise), natural products (resveratrol), drugs (metformin), or hormones (ghrelin, adiponectin).
source: It is important to note that AMPK is activated by metabolic stresses (fasting, exercise), but also by some natural products (resveratrol), drugs (metformin), or hormones (ghrelin, adiponectin) (Hardie, 2015; López, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hardie, 2015 and López, 2018

claim: In neurons, AMPK is phosphorylated and activated by the calcium sensor CaMKK in response to membrane depolarization.
source: Moreover, in neurons AMPK is also phosphorylated and activated by the calcium sensor CaMKK in response to membrane depolarization
evidence: Based on established knowledge of AMPK regulation in neurons

claim: CPT1C and protrudin form stable complexes in the ER.
source: We propose that both proteins form stable complexes in the ER, since glucose depletion or TOFA treatment does not separate them
evidence: Inferred from the observation that their interaction is not affected by metabolic stress

claim: CPT1C regulates protrudin through its N-regulatory domain.
source: We speculate that this regulation is mediated through the N-regulatory domain of CPT1C, which is a peptide of 50 residues that can adopt two different conformations (Nα and Nβ) as determined by NMR spectroscopy (Rao et al., 2011; Samanta et al., 2014)
evidence: Speculative statement based on NMR data from citations

claim: The N-regulatory domain of CPT1C switches between two conformations (Nα and Nβ) depending on malonyl-CoA levels.
source: This N-regulatory domain switches between the two conformations depending on malonyl-CoA levels
evidence: Based on established knowledge from NMR studies

claim: CPT1C and ORP1L show similarities in their mechanism of regulating LE/Lys transport by sensing nutrients and changing conformation.
source: This proposed mechanism shows similarities with the regulation of LE/Lys transport by ORP1L-sensing of cholesterol (Rocha et al., 2009; Wijdeven et al., 2015). Both CPT1C and ORP1L would act as nutrient sensors that regulate LE/Lys transport by changes in their own conformation
evidence: Inferred by comparing CPT1C mechanism to known ORP1L mechanism from citations

claim: The energetic regulation of LE/Lys plus-end transport mediated by CPT1C is of particular importance for corticospinal neurons.
source: The energetic regulation of LE/Lys plus-end transport mediated by CPT1C seems to be of particular importance for corticospinal neurons, the ones with longer axons in the body, since individuals carrying the missense CPT1CR37C or the nonsense CPT1CQ76X mutations develop HSP (Hong et al., 2019; Rinaldi et al., 2015)
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1C mutations cause HSP, which affects corticospinal neurons

claim: Arg37 is predicted to establish an electrostatic interaction with Glu3, stabilizing the Nα state of CPT1C.
source: Arg37 is predicted to establish an electrostatic interaction with Glu3, stabilizing the Nα state of CPT1C
evidence: Based on structural analysis and prediction

claim: The Arg37Cys mutation increases the distance between Arg37 and Glu3 and probably avoids the formation of the electrostatic interaction.
source: The loss of positive charge in Arg37Cys mutation increases the distance between the two residues and probably avoids the formation of the electrostatic interaction (Figure 10—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1

claim: The Arg37Cys mutation favors the extended conformation (Nβ state) of CPT1C.
source: This would favour the extended conformation (Nβ state), leaving CPT1CR37C in the malonyl-CoA-unbound state, which would explain why R37C mutation results in reduced axon growth
evidence: Inferred from structural predictions and experimental observations of reduced axon growth

claim: This is the first time that an energetic intermediate, such as malonyl-CoA, has been implicated in the regulation of LE/Lys transport.
source: This is the first time that an energetic intermediate, such as malonyl-CoA, has been implicated in the regulation of LE/Lys transport
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature review

claim: Protrudin is an important effector of CPT1C.
source: We find that protrudin is an important effector of CPT1C; although we cannot exclude that other mechanisms could be involved
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing CPT1C effects depend on protrudin

claim: Under normal nutrient conditions, CPT1C enhances protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to FYCO1 at the LE/Lys membrane, favoring plus-end transport.
source: Under normal nutrient conditions, CPT1C would enhance protrudin-mediated transfer of kinesin-1 to FYCO1 at the LE/Lys membrane, favoring plus-end transport
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments

claim: When glucose is not available or malonyl-CoA levels decrease, CPT1C changes its N-terminal conformation and slows down the plus-end transport of LE/Lys.
source: By contrast, when glucose is not available to cells or malonyl-CoA levels decrease, CPT1C would change its N-terminal conformation and slowdown the plus-end transport of LE/Lys preventing them to reach the axon tip and temporarily stop axon growth
evidence: Summarizes findings and proposes mechanism based on experimental data

claim: CPT1C regulation of LE/Lys transport is of special importance in neurons with long axons, such as corticospinal motor neurons.
source: This regulation seems of special importance in neurons with long axons, such as corticospinal motor neurons, since individuals with mutated CPT1C develop hereditary spastic paraplegia
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CPT1C mutations cause HSP affecting corticospinal neurons

claim: Anterograde transport of late endosomes or lysosomes (LE/Lys) is crucial for proper axon growth.
source: Anterograde transport of late endosomes or lysosomes (LE/Lys) is crucial for proper axon growth
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing established knowledge

claim: Malonyl-CoA is a precursor of fatty acids.
source: Malonyl-CoA is a precursor of fatty acids, and its intracellular levels highly fluctuate depending on glucose availability or the energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)
evidence: Based on established biochemical knowledge

claim: Intracellular malonyl-CoA levels highly fluctuate depending on glucose availability or AMPK.
source: Malonyl-CoA is a precursor of fatty acids, and its intracellular levels highly fluctuate depending on glucose availability or the energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)

claim: In HeLa cells, CPT1C senses malonyl-CoA and enhances LE/Lys anterograde transport by interacting with protrudin.
source: We demonstrate in HeLa cells that carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1C (CPT1C) senses malonyl-CoA and enhances LE/Lys anterograde transport by interacting with the endoplasmic reticulum protein protrudin and facilitating the transfer of Kinesin-1 from protrudin to LE/Lys
evidence: Summarizes findings from experiments in HeLa cells

claim: CPT1C facilitates the transfer of Kinesin-1 from protrudin to LE/Lys.
